To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the interfacial fluctuations are strongly suppressed by the wedge geometry, (ii) the critical exponent of the interfacial width, which is defined by the variance of the interface position, is 0.5, and (iii) the interfacially averaged height-height correlation function decays algebraically with a critical exponent that depends on the filling angle.

the interface critical exponents can be obtained from the one-dimensional approximation, that the interfacial fluctuations are described by mean-field theory, and that both the interface critical experiments and the short-distance fluctuations can be described within a single theory.

the short-distance fluctuations in a wedge-shaped substrate with an interface at its center are described by the same critical exponents as the one-dimensional approximation, and by the same mean-field exponents as in the bulk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interfacial fluctuations of an interface near the critical filling of a wedge-shaped substrate.
the critical behavior of the interface spanning a wedge shaped substrate.
the interplay of short-distance and long-distance fluctuations in the vicinity of the critical filling transition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the interface is a one-dimensional object with respect to its critical fluctuations but not with respect to its short-distance behavior.
the interfacial fluctuations are determined by two different length scales.
the short-distance interfacial fluctuations are governed by a mean-field theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interfacial fluctuations in the vicinity of a critical point can be described by the same critical exponents as the fluctuations at the critical point, but with a modified correlation length.
the interfacial fluctuations near a critical filling transition are described by two length scales, one for the long-distance fluctuations and one for the short-distance fluctuations.
the interfacial roughness is not a smooth function of the filling fraction, but rather exhibits a discontinuous jump.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while mean-field theory is a good approximation for short distances, the one-dimensional approach is more accurate for the long-distance behavior.
the mean-field theory is valid for the interfacial fluctuations in the wedge-shaped geometry at the critical filling transition.
, in contrast to the case where the substrate is planar, the interfacial fluctuations in the wedge are not Gaussian.
